📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Russian national has been indicted on suspicions he was a Russian spy who stalked and surveilled employees of a Silicon Valley firm that was assisting Ukraine in its ongoing war with its eastern neighbor.

Sources indicate that igor D’iu, 25, allegedly photographed the employees and their computer screens as they worked at a coffee shop located near the tech giant’s Palo Alto office, federal prosecutors mentioned Wednesday. He also kept a list of home addresses of employees and a senior executive. At one point, prosecutors said, D’iu trailed an employee as she traveled home from Palo Alto to San Francisco. An affidavit filed in the case referred to the employee as FEMP1, short for female employee, and said the event left her “in a state of emotional distress.”.

“FEMP1 made evasive and irregular turns, took back roads, and turned into a grocery store parking lot where D’IU continued aggressively following her vehicle,” an FBI special agent wrote. “D’IU followed FEMP1 through U-turns, illegal left turns, and ran a red light to stay with FEMP1 for nearly thirty miles. FEMP1 called 911 while driving and was instructed to drive directly to San Francisco Police Department (“SFPD”) Mission Station. Near SFPD Mission Station, FEMP1 flagged an SFPD patrol vehicle and reported the incident. D’IU left once FEMP1 made contact with the patrol vehicle.”.

When police later questioned D’iu about the incident, the defendant allegedly mentioned he saw a woman get into a car and thought she was “beautiful.” He then told the investigators that he followed her because he “wanted to ask her out on a date.”.

Prosecutors didn’t name the tech giant, but both Reuters and Bloomberg, citing unnamed people with knowledge of the case, identified it as Palantir. Ars is unable to confirm that reporting. Palantir representatives didn’t respond to an email seeking confirmation.

Sources indicate that D’iu allegedly entered the US unlawfully in the summer of 2026 after being recruited by someone over Telegram. Prosecutors said the party gave D’iu a clandestine assignment to target employees of a large technology and defense company. D’iu received instructions, equipment, and financial support along with information that his work was on behalf of “the motherland.” His instructions were to collect information about the company because it was supplying weapons for use against Russian forces in Ukraine.

Prosecutors said D’iu traveled from Istanbul, Turkey, to Mexico City in June. He then crossed the border into the US and was instructed to buy laptops, cell phones, wireless networking equipment, and remote access software. Besides instructions to monitor company employees at the coffee shop, D’iu’s orders also included positioning his laptop at certain locations near the company so it could be remotely accessed in an attempt to collect information from company employees nearby.

Recent findings suggest that D’iu allegedly obtained fraudulent identification documents to conceal his identity as he conducted his activities. The documents included a falsified California ID card, an altered US passport, and a Social Security card bearing the assumed name of “Hugo Landry Johns.” The passport was allegedly an authentic US passport that originally had been issued to someone elsewhere in the country. It was modified to display D’iu’s photograph and assumed identity.

Recent findings suggest that D’iu was arrested on October 30 and remains in custody. He is charged with one count of Conspiracy to Act as an Agent of a Foreign Government, one count of Acting as an Agent of a Foreign Government Without Notice to the Attorney General, and one count of Interstate Stalking. If convicted for Acting as an Agent of a Foreign Government Without Notice to the Attorney General, he faces a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison, a fine of $250,000, and three years of supervised release. He faces a maximum sentence of five years in prison, a fine of $250,000, and three years of supervised release for each conviction on the other two charges.

According to recent reports, D’iu had his initial appearance in federal court on November 2. He is next scheduled to appear in federal court on November 24.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon S3 Vectors now supports up to 40 KB of filterable metadata per vector, up from 2 KB.
  • S3 Vectors provides native support to store and query vectors in Amazon S3, delivering purpose-built, cost-optimized vector storage and query at billion-vector scale.
  • It has been revealed that the higher filterable metadata limit is available at no additional cost in all AWS Regions where Amazon S3 Vectors is available.

Amazon S3 Vectors now supports up to 40 KB of filterable metadata per vector, up from 2 KB. You can attach and filter on more attributes per vector, such as category, permissions, timestamps, and descriptive tags, so your retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), agentic, and semantic-search applications can narrow results by more of the fields that matter to them.

S3 Vectors provides native support to store and query vectors in Amazon S3, delivering purpose-built, cost-optimized vector storage and query at billion-vector scale. With this launch, indexes in new vector buckets support the higher limit by default, with no change to how you write vectors with PutVectors or run filtered queries with QueryVectors. To use the higher limit on an existing index, upgrade it in place to enhanced index mode with the UpdateIndexMode API.

It has been revealed that the higher filterable metadata limit is available at no additional cost in all AWS Regions where Amazon S3 Vectors is available. To get started, use the AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or the Amazon S3 console. To learn more, visit the Amazon S3 Vectors documentation.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the wake of the Make America Healthy Again movement’s midterm wipeout, a top leader suggested the heavy losses came down to being outspent by wealthier, more powerful rivals.
  • The dive into the financial documents reveals that the MAHA PAC, led by Tony Lyons, spent more on allies, boosters, meals, luxuries, and its affiliated nonprofit than it did on political candidates.
  • According to recent reports, the findings are in stark contrast to an announcement from Lyons in the spring that he was heading a $100 million fundraiser to boost MAHA’s clout in the midterms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the wake of the Make America Healthy Again movement’s midterm wipeout, a top leader suggested the heavy losses came down to being outspent by wealthier, more powerful rivals. But a Stat report on MAHA’s own spending in the run-up to the election raises questions about whether the group’s priority was ever winning elections in the first place.

The dive into the financial documents reveals that the MAHA PAC, led by Tony Lyons, spent more on allies, boosters, meals, luxuries, and its affiliated nonprofit than it did on political candidates.

According to recent reports, the findings are in stark contrast to an announcement from Lyons in the spring that he was heading a $100 million fundraiser to boost MAHA’s clout in the midterms. In reality, MAHA PAC took in $3.2 million. During the election cycle, the PAC spent more than $10.5 million, with over $7 million coming from money it had collected previously.

According to Stat’s findings, of the $10.5 million the MAHA PAC spent on the midterms, less than a tenth—roughly $1 million—went to messaging on political candidates, which are expenses called “independent expenditures.”.

Andrew Mayersohn, a committees researcher at OpenSecrets, called the spending “pretty unusual,” explaining that “Major super PACs spend most of their money on independent expenditures.”.

In a recent development, in some cases, the scant political spending was dwarfed by spending on luxuries. For instance, in a key House race in Northern California, MAHA supported Kevin Kiley over his political rival, pediatrician Richard Pan. Despite calling the race “the most direct ideological confrontation” between MAHA and its opposition “anywhere on the 2026 ballot,” the PAC only spent $49,900 to back Kiley. That’s a little less than the $50,100 it spent at Mastro’s Steakhouse, an upscale restaurant that offers $110 porterhouse steaks in Washington, DC. Further, it’s less than a third of the $155,900 the PAC spent at Ned’s Club, a luxury club near the White House that has become a popular gathering spot among Trump officials.

Kiley lost the election to Pan by double digits.

Industry observers note that of the roughly $1 million spent on political candidates, most of it—over $700,000—went to defeating Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.). Many other MAHA-endorsed candidates received $50,000 or less. Some got less than $2,000.

It has been revealed that outside of steaks and a private club, the MAHA PAC spent $500,000 on a media tech giant, Merit Street Media, run by Phil McGraw, who hosted a MAHA special featuring Dr. Phil. MAHA leaders used PAC money to cover meals, payroll, and credit card bills. The PAC paid $275,000 to a security firm, Gavin de Becker & Associates, which is led by an ally of anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., MAHA’s top leader. Tens of thousands more went to LLCs that have little to no online information.

On the other hand, prominent online MAHA influencers also pocketed tens of thousands from the PAC, as did writers for The MAHA Report, a Substack that promotes Kennedy and MAHA interests. In the days after the midterms, as members of the movement were coming to grips with the election losses, The MAHA Report chose to publish a lengthy article defending convicted rapist Russel Brand, a Kennedy ally who became a MAHA fixture.

Sources indicate that the biggest chunk of the MAHA PAC’s spending—more than $3 million—went to the nonprofit MAHA Action, which is also run by Lyons. It’s unclear how all that money was spent.

Builders using the newly introduced AWS experience on the Paid plan can now receive spend limit alerts by text message (SMS), alongside existing email notifications. A spend limit sets the maximum monthly cost for a project. Notifications are sent as a project approaches its limit, and when a project reaches its limit, AWS automatically pauses it. SMS gives builders a second way to stay informed about their project costs.

Recent findings suggest that email alerts can go unnoticed when builders are away from their inbox, leaving little time to respond before a project is paused. SMS alerts close this gap with a text message when a project's actual costs reach 90% of its spend limit, so builders have time to act, such as raising the limit or stopping resources they don't need.

Sources indicate that to turn on SMS alerts, verify your mobile phone number in AWS Settings and turn on text alerts for spend limits. Text alerts are only sent to verified numbers, and you can opt out at any time. SMS alerts for spend limits are available at no additional charge for US phone numbers, including Puerto Rico, Guam, the US Virgin Islands, and American Samoa.

To learn more, see Create a spend limit in AWS Settings, the AWS Account Management Reference Guide, or Get started with AWS.

Amazon fights the Delivery Protection Act with homepage banner, in-app pop-up

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In an unprecedented move, Amazon is using its app and website to try to convince shoppers to not support a Latest York City bill.
  • I also saw a smaller version of the notice on an order confirmation page on Amazon’s website.
  • Industry observers note that amazon is referring to Introduction 0518-2026 ( 518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In an unprecedented move, Amazon is using its app and website to try to convince shoppers to not support a Latest York City bill.

I also saw a smaller version of the notice on an order confirmation page on Amazon’s website. The message is delivered as a pop-up for users of the Amazon app, Bloomberg reported. Amazon hasn’t specified whether the messaging targets NYC residents based on addresses saved in their Amazon account or uses other techniques, such as device location services, but I only see the banner if I’m logged in to Amazon.

Industry observers note that amazon is referring to Introduction 0518-2026 ( 518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. If passed, it would require Amazon to directly employ the third-party delivery contractors that it uses.

Clicking on “Act now” on Amazon’s homepage or in the app brings up a page that gives shoppers a way to contact their NYC Council member and further states:.

It has been revealed that right now, Amazon works with a network of small delivery businesses that are deeply embedded in your communities. If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city. That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in Fresh York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.

It’s not unusual for Amazon to take a stance on political matters, and it has publicly opposed the Delivery Protection Act since April. What is fresh is Amazon using its online marketplace to push a political view. It’s uncommon to see a pop-up about legislation when visiting a shopping website.

Recent findings suggest that the messaging suggests that Amazon is concerned about the potential impact the proposed law would have on its costs. Besides Amazon, the bill targets any tech giant with last-mile delivery facilities in NYC, like FedEx and DoorDash.

Sources indicate that it also raises questions about the potential impact on shoppers should Amazon expand its use of its e-commerce platform for additional political messaging. The pop-up launched today impacts only NYC residents but sets a precedent for Amazon to sway political views on other issues. Amazon has made similar moves internally, including reportedly using an app for its employees to campaign against unionizing. But the new pop-up reveals Amazon extending that strategy directly to its consumers.

Given Amazon’s considerable influence in commerce, other companies could copy its actions. Uber and Lyft have previously done so, CNBC reports.

According to recent reports, finally, there’s the question of whether Amazon is fairly depicting the situations surrounding the bill. Notable supporters of the Delivery Protection Act include NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the Amazon division of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters. Using a platform with massive reach to communicate only one side of an ongoing debate could lead to misinformation and a skewed public perception.

Sources indicate that the Delivery Protection Act is currently stalled in the City Council’s Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection. The last hearing on the bill was in April. A committee vote on whether to advance the act to the full City Council hasn’t been set.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AWS Partner Central Agents now help AWS Partners create and manage AWS Partner Central and AWS Marketplace support cases in one place.
  • Partners can handle a case from start to finish in one chat, with the full record in AWS Support Center.
  • Recent findings suggest that the new support experience is available today to all AWS Partners and AWS Marketplace sellers in the AWS Partner Central console and through the AWS Partner Central Agents MCP server.

AWS Partner Central Agents now help AWS Partners create and manage AWS Partner Central and AWS Marketplace support cases in one place. The agents are available 24/7 and draw on Partner Central account details and authoritative, partner-specific knowledge from AWS to resolve most inquiries instantly. If a inquiry needs a support engineer, the agents will gather details and create a case. This reduces the time partners spend looking for help, and gives support teams the context they need to resolve cases faster.

Partners can handle a case from start to finish in one chat, with the full record in AWS Support Center. To create a case, partners can start describing their issue to AWS Partner Central Agents or use the prompt "get support." The agents gather additional details necessary to resolve the case, set the category, and draft the description. Partners review and submit the case, and the agents route the case to the right support team. In the same chat, partners can view case communications, track progress, post replies, and add attachments. With this launch, Partner Central and AWS Marketplace cases also move to AWS Support Center. There, partners can view the full case history and translate support correspondence into Chinese, French, German, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.

Recent findings suggest that the new support experience is available today to all AWS Partners and AWS Marketplace sellers in the AWS Partner Central console and through the AWS Partner Central Agents MCP server. With the MCP server, partners can bring the support experience into tools such as Kiro, AWS Quick, CRM systems, and other AI clients. To learn more, see Getting support in AWS Partner Central, Getting support for AWS Marketplace, and Getting started with the Partner Central Agents MCP server.

#18401. Latest Update: Trump admin still won't let Wi-Fi giant TP-Link sell its latest routers in US

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3713 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Trump admin still won't let Wi-Fi giant TP-Link sell its latest routers in US

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3713 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn’t allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US.
  • The rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US.
  • According to recent reports, while some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn’t allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US. The Trump administration imposed a sweeping ban on foreign-made consumer routers in March 2026, and TP-Link hasn’t been able to obtain an exemption.

The rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US. The Trump administration has control over which router makers receive special permission to import and sell new products through a waiver-review process involving the Federal Communications Commission, the Department of Defense, and the Department of Homeland Security.

According to recent reports, while some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials. Its routers approved before the March 2026 ban remain available for sale in the US, but its newly released Wi-Fi 8 routers cannot be imported or sold.

TP-Link’s struggle is not much of a surprise, given its history as a Chinese firm and the Trump administration’s focus on reducing reliance on Chinese and other foreign technology. While TP-Link faces political challenges related to the Trump administration’s push for on-shoring, its problems go deeper: It must convince the government its routers aren’t vulnerable to foreign hacking campaigns and that its routers are not Chinese-controlled technology, as suggested at a congressional committee hearing last year.

According to recent reports, TP-Link was founded in 1996 in China but has since split into two companies, with one in the US. The US-based TP-Link established California as its global headquarters in October 2024, months after completing a “formal organizational separation” from the TP-Link entity in China.

“TP-Link has split from and no longer has any affiliation with TP-LINK Technologies Co., Ltd., which serves the mainland Chinese market. Despite having similar names, these companies have entirely different ownership, management, and operations,” TP-Link claims.

TP-Link opened preorders for its first Wi-Fi 8 router, the Archer 8 Ultra, in September, though not in the US. It’s expected to ship this month and costs £899.99 in the UK, or about $1,178. Since it’s priced like a luxury device, its unavailability in the US won’t make a difference to most consumers. But it’s unknown how long it will take TP-Link to gain permission to sell Wi-Fi 8 routers in the US, or whether it will receive permission at all.

TP-Link has pledged to assemble all new routers in the US, but convincing Trump officials that it is fully under US control is likely a difficult task. The government reviews of router makers’ requests for waivers, formally called conditional approvals, are shrouded in secrecy. From the outside, it is unclear whether the Trump administration applies consistent security criteria to all companies or whether it grants waivers to favored companies without regard to the actual security of their products.

Companies led by Trump allies Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos fared well in the reviews. SpaceX’s Starlink division obtained a waiver for its routers, while Amazon received a waiver covering routers for its Leo satellite broadband service and the devices sold by its Eero subsidiary. There have been 26 waivers issued so far, covering products made by firms such as Netgear, Asus, Adtran, Calix, Nokia, Micro-Star International, Askey, Zyxel, Humax, and Vantiva.

Sources indicate that some US lawmakers seem to think the FCC process covers too many products. House Commerce Committee Ranking Member Frank Pallone, Jr. (D-N.J.) and Chairman Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.) proposed legislation in September that would limit the FCC’s authority to place entire categories of equipment on the list of banned products, as it did with routers.

Industry observers note that the Pallone/Guthrie bill would also require the FCC to report to Congress a week before adding any fresh technology or service to what’s known as the Covered List and require new additions to include only technologies or services produced or provided by an entity controlled by a foreign adversary. That means China, Russia, North Korea, or Iran.

“The current process for identifying and barring malicious foreign technology has worked in many cases, but lacks the transparency, consistency, and clarity needed to meet our long-term national security needs as technology rapidly advances,” Pallone and Guthrie stated in a joint statement.

Sources indicate that the Pentagon declined Ars’ request for comment on TP-Link’s request for an exemption. The FCC and Department of Homeland Security did not provide any comment.

It has been revealed that the US ban on all foreign routers was part of a dramatic expansion of the Covered List, which is managed by the FCC in consultation with the Commerce Department and federal agencies with national security expertise. The Covered List was created by a 2020 law and received its first additions in March 2021. It applies to products that “pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States or the security and safety of United States persons.”.

Recent findings suggest that for the first few years of the Covered List’s existence, only specific companies were added. This included Chinese device-makers Huawei and ZTE, several video surveillance product makers, the Russian security company Kaspersky Lab, and several Chinese telecom companies. Under the Trump administration, upcoming additions to the list include entire product categories, regardless of whether a particular vendor has been identified as a risk. In addition to routers, the Covered List presently includes foreign drones, robotic devices, and power inverters.

A former government official told Ars that the Covered List isn’t as useful as it should be.

“The government needs to be able to promptly identify national security risks and, to the extent that they can, you’ve got to give the public and industry guidance on what to do in order to avoid that risk,” said Betsy McIntyre, a lawyer and consultant who previously worked for the FCC on telecom mergers and at the Department of Justice on national security reviews of foreign investment in telecom. “That’s why I have always loved the Covered List. It’s this great tool. It’s simple. It has so much potential to guide procurement decisions for small businesses, large businesses. It can even help when moms are going to Best Buy and figuring out what kinds of equipment they should be buying.”.

McIntyre doesn’t like the approach of adding entire categories of products to the list, rather than specific products from individual companies.

“The ideal Covered List would be, as soon as there’s a problem, it would be updated,” she said. “They’d name a tech giant, and then people know: ‘don’t buy this’ or ‘this kind of equipment poses a national security risk.’ It’s a little bit muddled now.”.

Although the FCC maintains the Covered List, McIntyre noted the FCC’s role was set up at the beginning to be “very ministerial.” The FCC would add companies or products to the list based on determinations by national security agencies, with the FCC having no discretion once it received a determination.

Sources indicate that mcIntyre noted that she was not privy to any of the discussions that led to the broad inclusion of routers this year. It’s not necessarily clear to the public why any particular item is added to the list or why any company receives an exemption, because “the national security decision-making process can be a black box,” she stated.

TP-Link routers formed the bulk of a botnet controlled by Chinese threat actors, Microsoft remarked in 2024. But TP-Link is far from the only router maker whose products have vulnerabilities. Routers made by US companies Cisco and Netgear were part of a botnet of devices hijacked by Chinese state-sponsored attackers in 2023, the Justice Department said after taking action to remove the malware.

Security expert Bruce Schneier said there’s no reason to think TP-Link routers are less secure than those of its competitors. “They’re all awful. They’re all equally awful,” he told Ars.

Computers and smartphones generally have strong security because companies like Apple, Google, and Microsoft “have massive security teams designing these things to be good in the first place and writing patches when flaws are found,” Schneier noted.

In a recent development, with routers, webcams, smart refrigerators, wireless drones, and Internet of Things devices in general, “there’s no one on staff to deal with a security vulnerability… These are just less secure devices because the economics of them doesn’t reward security. The way you patch a lot of your home routers is you throw it away and buy a new one. That’s the patch mechanism.”.

When asked about TP-Link facing more scrutiny because of its history as a Chinese firm, Schneier said that router makers are “all Chinese companies… I don’t care what [name] you stick on the box. They’re all made in China.”.

TP-Link is pledging to assemble routers in the US, though it would still use parts from overseas. Schneier stated that “these are distinctions that don’t matter that much.”.

In a recent development, TP-Link claims the devices it sells in the US are made in Vietnam. But an April 2025 Bloomberg article said, “TP-Link confirmed that, aside from components bought in Vietnam that account for 0.5 percent of the total value of inputs to the plant there, all other components are imported from China.”.

TP-Link declined an interview request from Ars this month. “Aside from what’s already out there, the company doesn’t have any new updates to share right now,” a TP-Link spokesperson told us.

It has been revealed that TP-Link could sue the government, but litigation can drag out for years. Drone makers have been subject to the same kind of FCC import ban since December 2025, and Chinese drone maker DJI sued the FCC in February. FCC and Justice Department lawyers urged the court to dismiss the lawsuit as “premature,” because the FCC hasn’t made a final decision on a petition that DJI filed with the FCC. The US government’s latest motion to dismiss the lawsuit is still pending with the Ninth Circuit appeals court, and the FCC hasn’t ruled on the petition for reconsideration that DJI filed in January.

According to recent reports, several developments over the past two years make it unsurprising that TP-Link hasn’t obtained a waiver. US officials reportedly considered a TP-Link ban due to national security risks during the final months of the Biden administration. The government separately probed TP-Link last year in an antitrust investigation reportedly focused on whether it sold goods below cost to gain a dominant share of the US router market.

The House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party held a March 2025 hearing on deterring China’s hacking attacks and improving what the committee called “America’s lackluster cyber defenses.” Rob Joyce, former director of cybersecurity for the National Security Agency, noted in testimony that China is “undercutting our market to deliver Chinese-controlled technologies into our homes” and named TP-Link as the prime example.

“TP-Link, the world’s largest manufacturer of commercial Wi-Fi and home routers, has grown to at least 60 percent of the US retail market for Wi-Fi systems and SoHo [Small Office and Home Office] routers compared with about 10 percent of the market at the start of 2019,” he said. “How have they achieved this miraculous growth? They appear to be selling at price points below profitability to drive out the western competition… TP-Link routers were among the various brands exploited by Chinese state-sponsored hackers in the massive Volt, Flax, and Salt Typhoon attacks… We cannot have the software for these prolific devices be written, updated, and controlled by a Chinese organization. By law, such a company is subject to the direction of the PRC [People’s Republic of China] Intelligence apparatus. This is a threat we cannot ignore.”.

TP-Link noted in a March 2025 response to Joyce’s comments that its “products are not ‘Chinese-controlled technology,’” that “all of TP-Link’s R&D operations globally are owned and controlled by TP-Link’s US headquarters,” and that “no government—including the PRC—has access to and control over the design and production of TP-Link routers.”.

Sources indicate that in 2023, the year before Biden administration officials reportedly considered a TP-Link ban, TP-Link boasted of being “the world’s No. 1 Wi-Fi product provider for 12 years running” based on analyst firm IDC’s tracking of worldwide shipments. More recently, TP-Link has argued that estimates of its dominance are wildly inflated, at least in the US.

TP-Link’s response to Joyce noted it held “a 36.6 percent unit share and a 31 percent dollar share of the US consumer router market during 2024.” The company says in a fact sheet that when routers provided to customers by Internet service providers are taken into account, “TP-Link’s market share of residential Wi-Fi router sales in North America in 2024 was under 10 percent.”.

Industry observers note that florida and three other states with Republican attorneys general sued TP-Link last month, alleging that it lied to consumers about connections to China and the risks of its routers being exploited by Chinese state hackers. A group of 21 Republican state AGs also sent a letter to the FCC, urging it to address alleged violations of state laws in its review of TP-Link’s waiver request. TP-Link told the FCC that the “heightened standard” demanded by state attorneys general “would be unattainable to TP-Link or any other router manufacturer in the world.”.

Last month, the FCC warned TP-Link that several of its existing routers exceeded power limits. These include devices already being used by US consumers, such as the Archer BE670 tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router.

“Based on our evaluation of the purchased samples, we have tentatively determined that TP-Link included false or incorrect information in its applications for these equipment authorizations; and these devices do not operate consistently with the parameters power levels [sic] submitted in the certification applications,” the FCC told TP-Link.

It has been revealed that TP-Link told Bloomberg that any routers exceeding power limits are an aberration and that the four products identified by the FCC account for less than one-third of 1 percent of the company’s total US unit sales this year. Nonetheless, the power-limit investigation related to TP-Link’s existing routers may be a bad sign for its chances of getting a waiver to import and sell Wi-Fi 8 routers.

TP-Link told reporter Dong Ngo that the FCC tests were “routine spot checks.” But FCC officials may have examined existing TP-Link devices because of the pending request for a waiver from the Covered List.

“Any time a organization has significant requests before the agency, it’s not unusual if the agency is making sure that the company is behaving in a manner the way they expect it to, complying with the rules,” remarked Jeremy Marcus, a lawyer who spent over 20 years in government in multiple roles, including deputy chief of the FCC Enforcement Bureau.

Industry observers note that marcus declined to discuss TP-Link specifically. He noted that the FCC Office of Engineering and Technology has ongoing market surveillance programs. But when a company has larger problems pending at the FCC, the Office of Engineering and Technology may “do their own due diligence to make sure that existing equipment is performing the way it’s authorized to,” he said.

Although TP-Link has since gone a bit quiet and declined an interview request from Ars, a company official previously spoke to other publications about the FCC waiver process. TP-Link corporate affairs officer Steve Kovsky told PCMag last month that “there isn’t a lot of clarity” in the government’s demands for US-built technology. Many components used in routers are only available from foreign countries, he noted.

“There are no published guidelines that say, ‘Well, it could be 25 percent US, or it could be 15 percent US,'” he noted. “Or what about, we buy our chipsets for these products from Qualcomm and Broadcom. Is that a US product?”.

Recent findings suggest that kovsky’s background is in corporate marketing and communications, and he started at TP-Link a year ago in a contracting role as a senior communications strategist and consultant. He was hired as the corporate affairs officer in June and has been the main public speaker on the tech giant’s attempts to get a Covered List waiver.

Industry observers note that kovsky expressed some optimism last month. “We have no problem with the FCC, and are really looking forward to pursuing this, and really setting the standard for transparency, and showing that we have the ability to perform and meet all of these criteria with flying colors,” Kovsky told PCMag. “I don’t know if every manufacturer could say the same thing.”.

It has been revealed that kovsky spoke to The Verge around the same time, defending the firm’s security. “We do not sell customer data or share it with any government ever,” he noted. “We never will. We do not allow backdoors in our products. We are not susceptible to malware or vulnerabilities to an extent that’s greater than any other manufacturer in this category, to my knowledge.”.

According to recent reports, kovsky also downplayed TP-Link’s router market share in the US. “It’s about 9 to 10 percent, which is like top three,” he remarked. “It’s a good number, but we do not have an overwhelming share of the US market.”.

Industry observers note that kovsky pleaded with government officials for a quick approval in a letter to the FCC last month. TP-Link is ready to make “a nearly $1 billion investment in America that would result in equipping existing US factories, and ultimately building new, highly automated manufacturing facilities, to start assembling next-generation Wi-Fi 8 routers in the United States as soon as next year, creating hundreds of new jobs,” he wrote. “TP-Link is proud of this proposal and is poised to unleash this investment upon a grant of its Conditional Approval application.”.

Because the Trump administration added virtually all routers to the Covered List, each router maker must obtain a determination from the Department of Defense or Department of Homeland Security that its routers do not pose unacceptable national security risks and present a initiative to establish or expand manufacturing in the US.

Router makers seeking conditional approvals must submit, among other things, details about which countries all of the components and software in its routers come from; details about parts that have only a single source and contingency intends if those suppliers become unavailable; locations of manufacturing and assembly; and a “quantitative assessment of supply chain concentration by country, expressed as both a percentage of total value and production volume.”.

Router makers must also provide a “justification on why any foreign manufactured router is not presently manufactured in the United States, including why these foreign sources were selected and whether alternatives exist,” and a “detailed, time-bound initiative to establish or expand manufacturing in the United States.”.

Although McIntyre would prefer that the list be focused on individual companies instead of entire product categories, she said others argue that the process benefits the US because it forces companies to think harder about where they obtain components from and to provide the government with on-shoring prepares.

“I have talked to people who say, ‘Listen, you do these entire class bans, and it’s really forcing companies to really think about their supply chain… You want to have as many of these routers made in the United States as possible, just because you have a little bit more control over what’s going into the router,’” she mentioned.

The FCC remarked the addition of routers was based on a determination by a White House-convened group of Executive Branch agencies with national security expertise, which said that “malicious state and non-state sponsored cyber attackers have increasingly leveraged the vulnerabilities in small and home office routers produced abroad to carry out direct attacks.” The agencies said that “routers in the United States must have trusted supply chains so we are not providing foreign actors with potential built-in backdoors to American homes, businesses, critical infrastructure, and emergency services.”.

It has been revealed that although the FCC has generally based Covered List inclusions on determinations by other agencies, McIntyre pointed out an exception. In January 2025, the Commerce Department issued a determination about the risk of connected car hardware and software being controlled by Chinese- or Russian-controlled entities and used its own authority to prohibit transactions involving Chinese or Russian vehicle-connectivity systems.

After the Commerce determination, the FCC sought comment from the public on whether to add the vehicles to the Covered List. “That is the only example I have found of the FCC doing anything other than just taking what they were given and putting it on the Covered List,” McIntyre mentioned.

Sources indicate that under the law, the FCC is required to base Covered List decisions on determinations by federal agencies with national security expertise, or the Department of Commerce. With connected cars, the FCC took public comment and has not added the vehicles to the list.

“We are not required to provide the opportunity for public input on updates to the Covered List under the Commission’s rules, and we have not done so in the past,” the FCC said in May 2025. “However, because this would be the first addition that does not include the names of specific entities, we believe that offering an opportunity for public input will help promote transparency and good governance.”.

Industry observers note that the FCC made its first Covered List addition that does not include names of specific entities seven months later, but for drones, not connected cars. The Pallone/Guthrie bill mentioned earlier in this article would limit or prevent future additions that don’t name specific entities.

“The placement on or removal from the list… of a class or category of information and communications technology or service without reference to an entity that produced or provided that technology shall be deemed a major rule” as defined in the Congressional Review Act (CRA), the bill indicates.

Industry observers note that the CRA lets Congress overturn certain federal actions, including major rules. Pallone and Guthrie’s bill announcement mentioned the Covered List process needs Congressional oversight and that their proposed “changes improve consistency and transparency around the FCC Covered List, ensuring that it targets foreign adversaries and is used as Congress intended to safeguard our national security.”.

Amazon SageMaker JumpStart now offers a model leaderboard to compare models on quality, speed, and cost

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (236 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon SageMaker JumpStart now offers a model leaderboard in Amazon SageMaker Studio.
  • Comparing models has usually meant reading model cards one at a time and relying on benchmark scores that different sources published under different conditions.
  • The JumpStart model leaderboard is available at no additional charge in all AWS commercial Regions where Amazon SageMaker Studio is available.

Amazon SageMaker JumpStart now offers a model leaderboard in Amazon SageMaker Studio. You can use it to compare foundation models side by side on throughput, latency, and cost, and then deploy or customize the model that fits your workload.

Comparing models has usually meant reading model cards one at a time and relying on benchmark scores that different sources published under different conditions. The JumpStart leaderboard puts consistent measurements in one view. AWS evaluates every model on three reasoning benchmarks, MASSIVE-Bench Hard, GPQA Diamond, and MMLU-Pro, using the same evaluation setup for each model. AWS also measures time to first token, throughput, and instance cost on SageMaker for each JumpStart deployment configuration. You can use all of the filters already available for JumpStart models, such as model provider, license, and input and output modality, to narrow the list. You can also choose a use case profile and an optimization goal (balanced, cost, latency, or throughput) to see the metrics for the configuration you plan to deploy. At launch, the leaderboard covers more than 70 LLMs from providers including Meta, Google, Qwen, IBM, and Arcee.

The JumpStart model leaderboard is available at no additional charge in all AWS commercial Regions where Amazon SageMaker Studio is available. To get started, open SageMaker JumpStart in SageMaker Studio and choose the Leaderboard view. To learn more, see JumpStart leaderboard methodology and read the launch blog post.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, Amazon CloudWatch reveals telemetry filtering for the CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on, so you can stop paying to ingest telemetry you don't use.
  • You can now set cluster-wide include and exclude lists for namespaces, metric names, and pod and node labels.
  • Telemetry filtering is available in version 8.0.0 and later of the EKS add-on and Helm chart, in all AWS Regions where CloudWatch supports OpenTelemetry metrics.

Today, Amazon CloudWatch reveals telemetry filtering for the CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on, so you can stop paying to ingest telemetry you don't use.

You can now set cluster-wide include and exclude lists for namespaces, metric names, and pod and node labels. Exclude the non-production namespaces you don't monitor, drop high-cardinality metrics by name, and keep only the labels you group by rather than every label on every resource. Because ingestion is billed per GB, collecting less lowers what you pay, and you can adjust filters with a single add-on configuration update as your clusters change.

Telemetry filtering is available in version 8.0.0 and later of the EKS add-on and Helm chart, in all AWS Regions where CloudWatch supports OpenTelemetry metrics. Telemetry sent through the add-on is charged at the Amazon EKS OpenTelemetry ingestion rate of $0.08 per GB. For details, see Amazon CloudWatch insights pricing.

To get started, see Amazon CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on in the Amazon CloudWatch User Guide.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s now been 21 years since I first published an article at Ars Technica. It has been the only home I’ve known as a writer, and it has been essential to my development from scientist to blogger to journalist. It’s no exaggeration to say that Ars has helped make me who I am today.

So, asking you to support Ars via a subscription is very personal (and a bit selfish) for me—I’d like to stay here! Jobs that give you this sort of independence, that let you both edit and write, are very rare in journalism, and I’m unlikely to find another. Helping secure Ars’ future through your support will mean I don’t have to.

According to recent reports, but I’d rather make a case for why you’ll benefit from supporting Ars. In fact, I’ll make three: the writing, the people, and the community.

Industry observers note that since my start here, the central mission of Ars has been the same: cover the news in a way that helps our readers understand the facts and why they’re vital. The landscape has shifted dramatically over that time—technology, science, and policy are very different from 21 years ago. But understanding those changes and why they happened matters. It matters for everything from what you should buy today to what the world you’re going to be living in 10 years from now will look like.

Industry observers note that I’ve had the privilege of helping to decide how to translate that mission to science coverage. That decision took place against an important backdrop: While most people value things like evidence and research, they often struggle to recognize how those are used to build a body of reliable scientific information. That struggle kind of made the decision for me. Putting people in the know means helping them understand how science works as a process, and why that can produce information about the world we can trust.

Focusing on that has made our science coverage different from most of what you can get elsewhere. We don’t just tell you what’s fresh in the world of science; we help you understand the history of the major questions, the breakthroughs that allow us to address old problems in new ways, and the clever ideas people have for how to extract reliable information from a noisy and chaotic Universe. I’d like to think our readers get more out of that sort of writing, and it’s worth supporting.

But I’d be giving you a very incomplete picture of things if I only talked about science. Everyone at Ars has had to think about what sort of stories and presentation fit best with our mission. While our writing is essential now, it’s the people behind it that will ensure that it remains vital no matter what other changes come our way in the coming decades. And I can say with more than a little confidence that Ars is full of people you can trust to keep it that way.

One reason you can trust that is that the people at Ars now are, in many cases, the same ones who were here when you first started reading the site. We have remarkably low turnover, especially at the higher levels in our organization. There are two reasons for that: Ars is incredibly well-managed, and the people here believe in our mission.

The former is key because it should assure you that the money we get from your subscription won’t be wasted on some ill-advised pivot to video, or whatever the next craze is. The latter matters because it’s the people here who make Ars what it is. I work with some of the most thoughtful people I have ever encountered, and they all care deeply about making our work informative and compelling. I have also been lucky enough to work with a large group of freelancers over the years, and I have nothing but good things to say about them. We work hard to make sure that, even when the name on the byline is unfamiliar to you, you can be confident that you’re getting the same quality of reporting.

All of them—the full-time staff and the freelancers—are smart, great writers and know their areas of expertise better than most people in this business. Like I’m sure you do, I learn a lot from what they write (unlike you, I also get the bonus of learning from them in our Slack channels).

Sources indicate that but it’s not just my fellow writers whom I’ve learned from. We’ve got one of the smartest communities on the Internet, with experts from pretty much every area we cover regularly contributing to the comments. In the discussions attached to my articles, I have regularly seen them fill in details I didn’t have space to mention, clarify things in response to other readers’ questions, and talk about related topics that didn’t really fit into the article. I’ve learned a lot from this, and I’m confident the rest of the readers have, too.

It has been revealed that it’s strange to say the opposite of one of the central dogmas of the Internet: Read the comments. But it’s something I’ve told our freelance writers pretty regularly.

In a recent development, we’ve kept things that way even as most other sites’ comments turned toxic and were shut off. That’s taken both an editorial commitment and lots of staff time spent moderating and engaging in community management. Those don’t come for free, so your subscriptions will help support that, too.

In a recent development, I hope you’ll consider signing up if you’re able. Beyond the financials, I know we all appreciate it as a sign we’re on the right track.

The transcript comes back in the response, or Transcribe can write it to an S3 location you choose. Pricing is $0.0070 per minute of audio, billed per second, with speaker diarization, language identification, custom vocabulary and channel identification included. Two-channel audio is billed once on file duration. PII redaction is available as an add-on.

Sources indicate that supports English, Spanish, French, Italian, German, Japanese, Portuguese, Korean and Chinese (Simplified, Traditional and Hong Kong). Available in US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Ireland, London, Frankfurt), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo, Seoul) and South America (São Paulo), with PII redaction available in all stated Regions except South America (São Paulo).

Breaking: Only the Seminole Tribe can offer online gambling in Florida—and they're furious at DraftKings

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last week, DraftKings asked a federal court in Florida to take over a lawsuit recently filed against it by the Seminole Tribe, opening another front in the nationwide online “swaps” debate.
  • This Florida case adds to an already complex subplot involving Indigenous tribes, some of which are challenging prediction markets, while others are trying to get in on the action themselves.
  • In the latest lawsuit, the Seminole Tribe contends that two of DraftKings’ current online offerings—the fantasy sports-style “Pick6” and the “Super App” sportsbook—are “illegal” in Florida.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last week, DraftKings asked a federal court in Florida to take over a lawsuit recently filed against it by the Seminole Tribe, opening another front in the nationwide online “swaps” debate.

This Florida case adds to an already complex subplot involving Indigenous tribes, some of which are challenging prediction markets, while others are trying to get in on the action themselves.

In the latest lawsuit, the Seminole Tribe contends that two of DraftKings’ current online offerings—the fantasy sports-style “Pick6” and the “Super App” sportsbook—are “illegal” in Florida.

The tribe argues that every such “wager that Defendants now accept through their illegal sportsbook siphons away revenue that funds both the Tribe’s and Florida’s public programs and government services.”.

It has been revealed that neither DraftKings nor its attorneys immediately responded to Ars’ request for comment. However, in a court filing, DraftKings says that its products available to Floridians are merely “fantasy sports and the trading of [financial] derivatives” and not gambling.

DraftKings notes that its “licensed sportsbook” operates in other states but “not in Florida.”.

According to recent reports, multiple companies, including DraftKings, claim that their “swaps” (a type of financial derivative) are, in fact, properly governed by a federal agency, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. Therefore, DraftKings argues, states cannot regulate this activity as gambling.

The Seminoles, a sovereign nation and a federally recognized tribe, have a deal with the State of Florida, known as the 2021 Gaming Compact. That 30-year contract allows the tribe to maintain what the tribe states is the “exclusive right to offer online sports betting throughout the State of Florida.” In exchange, this betting regime is regulated, and Florida takes a cut.

But since that contract was signed, attorneys for the Seminole Tribe say in the complaint, DraftKings has pursued years of court challenges and a failed ballot measure designed to break into the Sunshine State.

As of 2026, DraftKings released “Pick6” in Florida, a game where individuals can put money down while predicting specific outcomes—for example, whether Victor Wembanyama of the San Antonio Spurs will score more or less than 28.5 points in his next basketball game.

Industry observers note that “Based on DraftKings’ representations, Florida consumers may predictably but incorrectly conclude that Pick6 is a legal product in Florida. It is not,” the complaint states.

“Pick6 is illegal ‘gambling’ under Florida law. DraftKings operates Pick6 without a license, without state oversight, and without any consumer protections Florida requires as a condition of legal sports wagering.”.

In June 2026, DraftKings released what it calls a “Super App,” which the Seminole Tribe argues is a “one-stop shop for illegal gambling,” as it provides an interface that is “in the same format used by every traditional, regulated sportsbook.”.

Florida-based professor Robert Jarvis of Nova Southeastern University studies gambling law, and he told Ars by email that he didn’t “buy the argument” DraftKings put forward that its products cannot be regulated under Florida gambling law.

Jarvis also noted that the tribe caught a break, too, with their randomly assigned federal judge.

“Not only have they had very good luck in federal court in previous cases, the federal judge assigned to the case is Ed Artau, who previously served as a Florida state trial judge (2014–20) and a Florida state appellate judge (2020–25),” he wrote. “Thus, in a sense, the Seminoles get the best of both worlds: a federal court run by a Florida state judge.”.

Sources indicate that amazon DynamoDB vector search inline filters now support range comparisons, value lists, and logical operators in addition to the equality operator, so you can narrow a vector search to exactly the items you want. You can now filter on numeric ranges such as price, rating, or publish date, match an attribute against a list of values, check whether an attribute exists, and combine conditions with OR and NOT. Amazon DynamoDB vector indexes store vector embeddings alongside your operational data, and the SearchVectors API returns the items whose embeddings are most similar to your query vector.

The search condition expression in a SearchVectors request now accepts the comparison operators <, <=, >, >=, and BETWEEN on Number attributes, the IN operator, the attribute_exists and attribute_not_exists functions, and the logical operators AND, OR, and NOT. DynamoDB applies the filter during the search, so every result it returns matches. For example, a retail application can return the products most similar to a shopper's query within a price range and a set of brands, and a retrieval-augmented generation application can limit results to selected document categories published after a given date.

The new operators are available in all AWS Regions where DynamoDB vector search is available.

To learn more, see vector search in the Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide, or visit the Amazon DynamoDB page.

Rocket Report: A weekend of ups and downs; Stoke celebrates engine milestone

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1994 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, welcome to Edition 9.20 of the Rocket Report!
  • Europe’s leading satellite startup eyes Italian rocket maker.
  • In a recent development, fulfilling a need … In a statement, ICEYE said it wants to join forces with Avio to meet Europe’s need for “sovereign space and defense capabilities.” ICEYE manufactures and operates its own satellites for radar surveillance and sells data to commercial customers and national governments, including Ukraine, which uses ICEYE imagery for targeting and tracking Russian troop movements.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, welcome to Edition 9.20 of the Rocket Report! Last weekend was a picture of the US launch business in miniature, and emblematic of the opposing trajectories of two of the nation’s most experienced rocket makers. First, on Saturday, SpaceX completed a perfect midair catch of its Starship upper stage at its launch pad in Texas after spending nearly a day in orbit. The Super Heavy booster was lost at sea, but SpaceX proved it can recover that piece of the rocket on previous flights. While SpaceX highlighted it is well on the way to fielding a fully reusable rocket, United Launch Alliance suffered its first-ever total launch failure with the Vulcan rocket. That is terrible news for not only ULA, but also the US Space Force and Amazon, which have booked some 70 releases on Vulcan over the next few years. Your faithful correspondents will take a break from the Rocket Report next week for the Thanksgiving holiday, so we’ll see you again the first week of December.

Europe’s leading satellite startup eyes Italian rocket maker. Finnish satellite developer ICEYE announced Tuesday that it is seeking to buy Italian rocket-maker Avio for more than $2.2 billion in a transaction aimed at creating Europe’s first true vertically integrated end-to-end space company, Ars reports. Avio builds the Vega C rocket, a solid-fueled launcher designed to carry up to 3.3 metric tons (7,300 pounds) of payload to low-Earth orbit. ICEYE is, by far, the most successful space startup in Europe, with a valuation of more than $12 billion after the company’s most recent fundraising round in June.

In a recent development, fulfilling a need … In a statement, ICEYE said it wants to join forces with Avio to meet Europe’s need for “sovereign space and defense capabilities.” ICEYE manufactures and operates its own satellites for radar surveillance and sells data to commercial customers and national governments, including Ukraine, which uses ICEYE imagery for targeting and tracking Russian troop movements. Most of ICEYE’s satellites have launched on SpaceX Falcon 9 rockets. With Falcon 9’s retirement on the horizon, ICEYE’s satellites will need rides to orbit. Avio’s Vega C rocket has a healthy backlog of contracts for European governments, but it hasn’t been a hit commercially. Investment from ICEYE could shore up Avio’s Vega rocket program and perhaps accelerate development of a upcoming rocket.

Recent findings suggest that NATO unveils launch brokerage initiative. The North Atlantic Treaty Organization is contracting commercial rockets and spaceports to grow its satellite launch network and help neutralize risks to the space systems on which it relies, Bloomberg reports. NATO released two initiatives on Tuesday: Starlift, through which participating countries can secure slots on commercial rockets, and the Global Data Marketplace, which will bolster the alliance’s military operations in space with commercial data and services.

It has been revealed that swimming in launches … Starlift will allow participating countries—Belgium, Canada, Finland, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, Turkey, the UK, and South Korea—to pool their military launch requirements and secure launch slots on commercial rockets. The NATO initiative will also prepare and test procedures for short-notice launches, as might be needed in a crisis. Bloomberg reported NATO’s tech agency will offer about $2.7 billion in contracts over the next two years, including to commercial space companies, AI, cyber, and command-and-control networks.

Industry observers note that stoke wraps up booster engine development. Stoke Space has completed development of its Zenith engine, the methane-fueled powerplant that will propel the manufacturer’s medium-class Nova rocket off the launch pad. Stoke made the announcement in a social media post Thursday. “As flight engines clear acceptance testing, we’re shipping them down to Cape Canaveral for integration with Nova’s first stage—every week,” Stoke said. Seven Zenith engines will power the Nova rocket’s reusable first stage booster, combining to generate about 700,000 pounds of thrust at full throttle.

Industry observers note that all eyes on Stage 2 … Stoke announced it cleared a “proto-qualification” milestone on Stage 1 earlier this year. Stage 2 is undergoing cryogenic proof testing and a hot-fire test campaign at Stoke’s test complex in rural Washington. Nova’s second stage is the real innovation, with a unique arrangement of 24 thrusters surrounding a regeneratively cooled heat shield to protect it during reentry back into Earth’s atmosphere. With this, Stoke aims to fully reuse both Nova stages. The first launch is presently expected sometime next year.

Sources indicate that soyuz flies from Russia’s Far East. A Soyuz-2.1b rocket made its first and only launch from Russia’s Vostochny Cosmodrome this year, RussianSpaceWeb.com reports. The rocket’s Fregat upper stage deployed a newly introduced pair of high-resolution imaging satellites, along with a cluster of smaller payloads, following liftoff from Russia’s Vostochny launch base on November 14 (local time). Vostochny, located in Russia’s Far East, hosted its first space launch in 2016. By some measures, Russia spent more than $5 billion building Vostochny, only to use it for an average of two rolls out per year.

What was onboard? … Soyuz and Fregat carried two dual-use imaging surveillance satellites. A pair of CubeSat-class satellites for a Russian arms manufacturer were also onboard. These satellites are owned by NPO Kaisant, which specializes in drone communications and counter-drone weapons. NPO Kaisant states the satellites will join a constellation providing secure communications to Russian drones over Ukraine. A total of 12 secondary payloads were reported to be onboard, according to Roscosmos.

China’s LandSpace reports rocket reuse milestone. Three months after landing its first orbital-class rocket booster, Chinese rocket manufacturer LandSpace claims it has completed “ground acceptance and testing” of the nine methane-fueled engines recovered from the first stage of its Zhuque-3 rocket, according to Guandian News, a Chinese outlet focusing on the country’s financial and economic sector. The engines were disassembled, inspected, refurbished, reassembled, and retested after flying to space and back in August.

But wait … LandSpace’s Zhuque-3 is one of two Chinese rockets to successfully land its booster after an orbital launch attempt. The company did not say whether any of the nine engines will fly again, but don’t count on the entire Zhuque-3 booster stage from the August flight making another trip to space. The Zhuque-3 first stage toppled over soon after a seemingly flawless touchdown at LandSpace’s downrange recovery zone in northwestern China. Based on this week’s news, it appears engineers were able to salvage the engines.

Sources indicate that spaceX makes a historic catch. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, took a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket with the first successful catch of its enormous Starship upper stage on November 14, Ars reports. It’s hard to overstate the significance of the moment. SpaceX’s ability to recover and quickly relaunch Starships and Super Heavy boosters is central to all of the company’s lofty commercial ambitions and many of America’s high-level strategic imperatives, from national security to maintaining dominance in space exploration.

Industry observers note that what was it like to be there? … Ars Space Editor Eric Berger covered the launch and catch of Starship from a nearby perch at Starbase, Texas. “Watching Starship launch from here a little less than a day earlier, and knowing it had orbited the planet multiple times, added to the sense of unreality in seeing this spaceship return to Earth under its own power and be captured by the tower,” Berger writes. “It felt like stepping into the future. SpaceX has dazzled us before by landing rockets on barges and returning humans to space with Crew Dragon. But this flight took things to another level. Starships are huge. They carry a huge amount of energy coming back from orbit. And until a few years ago, it seemed beyond fantastical to think about capturing a rocket with what are essentially outsized chopsticks. Nevertheless, it happened.”.

Industry observers note that vulcan fails to deliver for Amazon. United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket and 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff Sunday, a crushing setback that will ripple across all sectors of the US space industry, Ars reports. Aside from ULA itself, the fallout from the failure will strike the US military and Amazon hardest. Sunday’s mission was the first of 38 Vulcan releases booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX’s Starlink. Vulcan is also on contract to launch roughly half of the US Space Force’s national security missions over the next few years.

Identifying the cause … ULA said Wednesday that the failure was caused by inadequate fuel supply to the first stage engines, Ars reports in a follow-up story. “ULA has completed an initial integrated review of flight data from the Leo 1 launch anomaly that occurred last Sunday,” the company said in a statement. “While work remains to determine cause, preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines.” This is fantastic news for Blue Origin, which builds the BE-4 and uses a similar design on its own Latest Glenn rocket. Vulcan’s solid rocket boosters also performed as expected Sunday after experiencing nozzle failures on two prior Vulcan flights.

Google taps Blue Origin for AI launch. Blue Origin announced Thursday that its Fresh Glenn rocket will launch data center satellites for Google in 2029 as part of that organization’s Project Suncatcher program, Ars reports. Google disclosed it was working on scalable orbiting data centers about a year ago and characterized the project as one of its research “moonshots.” The mission on New Glenn is designed to deploy satellites, each with computing capacity at roughly the scale of a data center rack, into Sun-synchronous orbit where they can receive nearly continuous solar energy.

In a recent development, hitching a ride … Google snatched up a ride on New Glenn just as US commercial heavy-lift rockets are filling up their capacity through the year 2030. The Google mission will fly on the 7×2 variant of the New Glenn rocket, the smaller version of the vehicle that has debuted three times to date. The purpose of the 2029 launch will likely be to test the ability to network solar-powered satellites equipped with AI chips and demonstrate machine-learning compute in space. Perhaps the bigger question for Google is not whether it can make this technology work—but whether it is tenable for a manufacturer to have ambitions for a large constellation of orbital data centers in the 2030s without its own launch vehicle.

According to recent reports, relativity makes progress with Terran R. Another new rocket is moving closer to the launch pad. Relativity Space’s partially reusable Terran R rocket could launch sometime next year if engineers can finish development with no major setbacks. Relativity posted an update on YouTube this week, detailing several recent achievements at several of the manufacturer’s locations across the country. At Relativity headquarters in Southern California, teams have completed Terran R’s first stage thrust structure with a full set of 13 Aeon engines, fluid lines, and avionics. The engine compartment is now being integrated with Stage 1 tankage. Terran R’s second stage recently completed its first all-up test firing at Stennis Space Center, Mississippi.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, at Cape Canaveral … Relativity is also moving forward with the Terran R launch pad at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida. The launch pad’s lightning protection towers are now complete, as is the steel framing for Terran R’s launch table. Work continues on the rocket’s transporter-erector, strongback, and the launch pad’s propellant storage tanks.

November 21: Falcon 9 | USSF-317 | Vandenberg Space Force Base, California | 02:32 UTC.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Applications instrumented with an OpenTelemetry SDK send to an OTLP endpoint that the agent serves on every node, on by default.
  • For Prometheus metrics, the agent scrapes the targets described by standard ServiceMonitor and PodMonitor objects, with no Prometheus operator to run and no change to your scrape configuration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that today, Amazon CloudWatch introduces support for your own application telemetry in the CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on. The CloudWatch agent you already run now accepts metrics, traces, and logs from your applications, so you don't deploy and operate a separate collector to get them into CloudWatch.

Applications instrumented with an OpenTelemetry SDK send to an OTLP endpoint that the agent serves on every node, on by default. Metrics arrive as CloudWatch metrics you query with PromQL, traces go to AWS X-Ray and Transaction Search, and logs go to CloudWatch Logs.

For Prometheus metrics, the agent scrapes the targets described by standard ServiceMonitor and PodMonitor objects, with no Prometheus operator to run and no change to your scrape configuration. Each team defines its own targets alongside its application rather than in one central add-on configuration. Label selectors let you choose which monitors CloudWatch scrapes.

Both sources carry the same Kubernetes, host, cloud, and service attributes the add-on applies to the pod they came from, so you can join application telemetry to your cluster metrics.

According to recent reports, custom telemetry is available in version 8.0.0 and later of the EKS add-on and Helm chart, in all AWS Regions where CloudWatch supports OpenTelemetry metrics. Telemetry is charged at the Amazon EKS OpenTelemetry ingestion rate of $0.08 per GB. For details, see Amazon CloudWatch insights pricing.

To get started, see Custom telemetry in the Amazon CloudWatch User Guide.

Today, AWS unveils the preview of Data Hub in AWS Billing and Cost Management, a managed data layer that enables AWS FinOps Agent to query cost and usage data with SQL. In preview, Data Hub is available to AWS FinOps Agent, so the agent can identify the individual resources behind a cost change, break down spend by team or cost allocation tag, and show how a resource's cost and usage change hour by hour. With AWS FinOps Agent and Data Hub, customers get these answers without setting up a data export or building and maintaining a cost data pipeline.

Data Hub provides 13 months of hourly, resource-level cost and usage data in the published CUR 2.0 schema, including resource identifiers and cost allocation tags. AWS provisions the data, refreshes data daily, and maintains the schema as fresh services, commitments, and charge types are added. When set up from the management account, Data Hub covers cost and usage data across the accounts in your organization.

According to recent reports, data Hub (preview) is available in the US East (N. Virginia) Region and covers cost and usage data across regions. There is no charge for Data Hub during preview.

To learn more about Data Hub, see the AWS Billing and Cost Management User Guide and the launch blog. You can get started from the Data Hub page in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console or from the AWS FinOps Agent console.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lenders backing SpaceX’s latest $43 billion debt package, which is secured by its advanced AI chips, have tried to bar Elon Musk from firing the collateral into space as part of his initiative for orbital data centers.
  • Sources indicate that the world’s richest man has outlined ambitious aims to power AI models with data centers cooled by the vacuum of space.
  • According to recent reports, spaceX has said it plans to use the chips involved in the debt deal on Earth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lenders backing SpaceX’s latest $43 billion debt package, which is secured by its advanced AI chips, have tried to bar Elon Musk from firing the collateral into space as part of his initiative for orbital data centers.

Sources indicate that the world’s richest man has outlined ambitious aims to power AI models with data centers cooled by the vacuum of space. That will require packing satellites full of advanced chips.

According to recent reports, spaceX has said it plans to use the chips involved in the debt deal on Earth. But lenders have expressed concerns that if the group later decided to shoot the valuable chips that underpin their loans into space, it would prevent them from reclaiming and selling the semiconductors in the event of a default, according to people familiar with the matter.

It is uncertain whether the provision was included in the finalized documents.

The bonds were issued by a special purpose vehicle designed to keep the debt off SpaceX’s balance sheet and preserve its investment-grade credit rating.

The proposed debt covenant presented potential legal challenges for SpaceX’s ambitions to build data centers in space, highlighting the uncharted territory that investors need to navigate when financing the nascent asset class.

SpaceX sold more than $30 billion of the debt to large investors on Thursday as part of a financing package dubbed “Project Saturn.” The largest portion of the debt package was a $25 billion investment-grade bond backed by SpaceX’s five-year lease payment for the Nvidia chips.

According to recent reports, the debt was sold at 3.45 percentage points above US Treasuries, indicating a total yield of about 8.3 percent, the people said. SpaceX’s corporate debt maturing in 2031, meanwhile, traded at a yield of about 7.2 percent on Thursday.

The newest bonds will mature in 2032, but the principal will be paid off in less than four years—an arrangement that was designed to reduce credit risks for lenders, the people added.

More than $19 billion of the bonds already secured commitments prior to Thursday, including $4 billion from Pimco.

Apollo and Goldman Sachs, which led the transaction, declined to comment. Pimco declined to comment. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.

Funds managed and advised by BlackRock, Goldman Sachs Asset Management, and KKR have also made anchor commitments in the transaction, according to SpaceX.

SpaceX plans to use the chips in US data centers majority-owned, controlled, and operated by SpaceX, according to a rating report issued by Moody’s.

Moody’s assigned the debt an A3 rating, one notch above SpaceX’s own credit rating. KBRA rated the debt A-minus.

The credit rating agencies attributed the A-tier rating in part to “hell-or-high-water” clauses that prevent SpaceX from walking away from the lease.

“The SpaceX GPU deal appears cleverly structured and should appeal to a panoply of buyers, potentially including deep pools of insurance capital seeking attractive yield on investment-grade debt,” stated Grant Nachman, chief investment officer at Shorecliff Asset Management.

“This transaction could prove a harbinger of future issuances,” he noted.

Additional reporting by Jill R Shah in Fresh York.

According to recent reports, AWS Quick now includes enterprise guardrails, giving administrators configurable content safety and sensitive-information controls for user prompts. Administrators can apply guardrail policies to individual people or enterprise identity provider (IdP) groups or set a policy as the account default. User-level policies take precedence over group policies and account defaults. When multiple group policies apply, Quick combines their content restrictions, using the stricter setting when controls overlap. Administrators create guardrail policies in the Quick administration console using content filters, denied topics, blocked words and phrases, prompt-attack detection, and controls for selected types of personally identifiable information (PII). For example, an administrator can create a policy that blocks prompts containing confidential project names and assign it to an IdP group. Detect-only mode lets administrators test prompt-filtering rules against real production traffic before enforcing them. In this mode, Quick evaluates user prompts and logs policy matches without blocking requests, so administrators can assess the impact on business workflows and refine policies. When administrators enable enforcement, Quick blocks matching prompts and displays a message to the user. Administrators can review detected and blocked events in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Enterprise guardrails are available in preview for select Quick customers with Professional and Enterprise intends. For feature availability by AWS Region, see AWS Quick Regions. To learn more, see the enterprise guardrails documentation.
